pos: n. (loss of sight; rendering Hebrew sanverim, Greek porosis)
etymology: From blind, Old English blind. Scripture's blindness is nearly always judicial or spiritual before it is medical.
biblical_def: Blindness is the loss of sight, and Scripture uses it chiefly of the soul. The men of Sodom are struck with it at Lot's door (Gen 19:11), and the Syrian army at Elisha's prayer (2Ki 6:18). Paul explains Israel's condition with it: “blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in” (Rom 11:25). Christ's verdict on the Pharisees inverts the categories: “if ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth” (Joh 9:41).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blindness as want of sight; and ignorance, intellectual darkness.
webster_full: BLINDNESS, n. Want of sight; want of a physical faculty of perceiving objects by the instrumentality of the eyes.
2. Ignorance; intellectual darkness.
scriptures: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.
Joh 9:41
Jesus said unto them, If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth.
And they smote the men that were at the door of the house with blindness, both small and great: so that they wearied themselves to find the door.
And when they came down to him, Elisha prayed unto the LORD, and said, Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness. And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.
corruption_summary: Spiritual blindness is assumed to be obvious to the blind, when Christ's whole point in John 9 is that the confident claim to see is the disqualifying symptom.
corruption_paragraphs: John 9 ends with a sentence that reverses every expectation. Christ says, For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind. The Pharisees ask, are we blind also? and He answers: if ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth. Admitted blindness is curable. Asserted sight is not, because a man who is certain he sees will not ask for eyes.

Romans 11:25 keeps the doctrine from becoming a weapon. Paul calls Israel's blindness partial, temporary, and purposeful — until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in — and prefaces it with a warning: lest ye should be wise in your own conceits. The Gentile church is told the exact history of its own grafting, so that no branch mistakes a temporary blindness in another for permanent superiority in itself.
roots_summary: Hebrew sanverim (H5575), a sudden dazzling blindness; Greek porosis (G4457), a hardening or callus — the New Testament's word is about hardening, not darkness.
roots_lines: Hebrew sanverim (H5575) — blindness by dazzling; Genesis 19:11, 2 Kings 6:18.
Greek porosis (G4457) — hardening, callousness; Romans 11:25, Ephesians 4:18, Mark 3:5.
Greek tuphloo (G5186) — to blind; 2 Corinthians 4:4, the god of this world hath blinded the minds.
usage: “Blindness in part is happened to Israel” — partial, temporary, purposeful.
“Now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth” — asserted sight is the disqualifier.
“They wearied themselves to find the door” — Sodom at Lot's threshold.

etymology: From Latin impotens, without power. The KJV uses it in its older, literal sense: physically incapable, not the modern narrowed meaning.
biblical_def: Impotent means without strength. It describes the crowd at Bethesda — “a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered” (Joh 5:3) — among whom lay a man who had been thirty-eight years in that condition and whom Christ asks, “Wilt thou be made whole?” (Joh 5:6). Peter heals an impotent man at the Beautiful gate and is examined about “the good deed done to the impotent man” (Act 4:9), and Paul perceives a cripple at Lystra has faith to be healed (Act 14:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impotent as weak, feeble, wanting strength or power; unable by nature, or disabled.
webster_full: IMPOTENT, a. Weak; feeble; wanting strength or power; unable by nature, or disabled by disease or accident.
2. Wanting the power of propagation.
3. Wanting the power of self-restraint; ungovernable.
scriptures: Joh 5:3
In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water.
Joh 5:6
When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?
Act 4:9
If we this day be examined of the good deed done to the impotent man, by what means he is made whole;
Act 3:6
Then Peter said, Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.
corruption_summary: Christ's question to a thirty-eight-year invalid — wilt thou be made whole? — is read as rhetorical, when it exposes how a long infirmity can become an identity.
corruption_paragraphs: The man at Bethesda does not answer the question he is asked. Christ says, Wilt thou be made whole? and he replies with an explanation of why he never gets into the water: Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool. Thirty-eight years had produced a settled account of his situation, and the account had a place for everyone in it except a healer standing in front of him. Christ heals him anyway, which is mercy, and then finds him later with a warning: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.

Acts 3 supplies the apostolic pattern and its honesty about resources. Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk. Peter does not pretend to means he lacks, and he does not apologize for the means he has. The church has often reversed both halves — embarrassed about the Name, confident about the budget.
roots_summary: Greek astheneo (G770), to be weak or sick; adunatos (G102), without power, impotent — the same word used of what is impossible with men.
roots_lines: Greek astheneo (G770) — to be feeble, sick; John 5:3, 7, and 2 Corinthians 12:10, when I am weak, then am I strong.
Greek adunatos (G102) — powerless, impossible; Acts 14:8, Romans 8:3, what the law could not do.
Greek hugies (G5199) — whole, sound; John 5:6, wilt thou be made whole?
usage: “A great multitude of impotent folk” — the porches of Bethesda.
“Wilt thou be made whole?” — a question a long infirmity struggles to answer.
“Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee” — honest about both.

etymology: From Greek lepros, scaly. The biblical condition covers a range of defiling skin diseases, and its legal consequence is separation.
biblical_def: Leprous describes one under the law's severest ceremonial exclusion: “he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be” (Lev 13:46). Moses' hand becomes “leprous as snow” and is restored as a sign (Exo 4:6). Miriam is struck for speaking against Moses (Num 12:10), Naaman is cleansed in Jordan (2Ki 5:14), and Uzziah is leprous to the day of his death for burning incense in the temple (2Ch 26:21). Christ touches a leper — the one thing the law forbade — and the man is cleansed rather than the Lord defiled (Mat 8:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines leprous as infected with leprosy; and covered with white scales.
webster_full: LEPROUS, a. Infected with leprosy; covered with white scales.
scriptures: All the days wherein the plague shall be in him he shall be defiled; he is unclean: he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be.
Mat 8:3
And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
And the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow: and Aaron looked upon Miriam, and, behold, she was leprous.
corruption_summary: Leprosy is reduced to a metaphor for sin, which is true but incomplete — the law's actual concern was contagion of holiness in reverse, and Christ's touch is what settles the direction.
corruption_paragraphs: Under the law, contact ran one direction: the clean thing touching the unclean became unclean. That is why the leper's habitation was outside the camp and why he cried Unclean, unclean. Matthew 8:3 breaks the physics without breaking the law: Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. The contagion reverses. Holiness proves the stronger substance, which is the gospel in one gesture.

Naaman's story guards against a second error. He expected a ceremony worthy of his rank and was told to wash seven times in a muddy provincial river, and he went away in a rage — are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? His servants' reasoning saved him: if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? The offence of a simple remedy is very old.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsara (H6879), to be struck with leprosy; tsaraath (H6883), the condition — applied also to garments and houses; Greek lepra (G3014).
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaraath (H6883) — leprosy; Leviticus 13-14, and of houses and garments as well as skin.
Greek lepros (G3015) — leprous; Matthew 8:2, 26:6, Simon the leper.
Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; Matthew 8:3, be thou clean.
usage: “Without the camp shall his habitation be” — the law's severest separation.
“He put forth his hand, and touched him” — the contagion runs the other way.
“Wash, and be clean” — the offence of a simple remedy.

pos: v. part. (taken from the breast; rendering Hebrew gamal)
etymology: Old English wenian, to accustom. Weaning is not deprivation but transition — the child is being accustomed to a different and better food.
biblical_def: Weaned describes a child taken from the breast. Abraham made a great feast the day Isaac was weaned (Gen 21:8), and Hannah waited until Samuel was weaned before bringing him to the house of the LORD (1Sa 1:22–24). David makes it the image of a settled soul: “Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child” (Psa 131:2). Isaiah asks whom the LORD shall teach knowledge — “them that are weaned from the milk” (Isa 28:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wean as to accustom and reconcile a child or other young animal to a want or deprivation of the breast; and figuratively, to detach from an accustomed object.
webster_full: WEAN, v.t. To accustom and reconcile, as a child or other young animal, to a want or deprivation of the breast.
2. To detach or alienate the affections from any object of desire; to reconcile to the want of any thing.
scriptures: Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child.
Gen 21:8
And the child grew, and was weaned: and Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned.
But Hannah went not up; for she said unto her husband, I will not go up until the child be weaned, and then I will bring him, that he may appear before the LORD, and there abide for ever.
Isa 28:9
Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand doctrine? them that are weaned from the milk, and drawn from the breasts.
corruption_summary: Contentment is sought as a feeling to be summoned, when Psalm 131 describes it as the settled state after a weaning — something that happens to a soul, usually against its will.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 131 is three verses long and describes an achieved quiet: LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me. Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother. The image is exact. A weaned child still sits with its mother but no longer for what it can get; the relationship has outgrown the transaction. That is the difference between a believer who wants God's gifts and one who wants God.

Weaning is also, in the moment, experienced as loss. The child does not understand that a better food is coming; it knows only that a familiar comfort has been withdrawn. Isaiah's connection is worth keeping in mind during such seasons: whom shall he teach knowledge? them that are weaned from the milk. Some instruction cannot be given to a soul still fed on what it must eventually leave behind.
roots_summary: Hebrew gamal (H1580), to deal fully with, to wean, to ripen — the same verb translated deal bountifully in the psalms.
roots_lines: Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to wean, to deal bountifully; Psalm 131:2, Genesis 21:8, and Psalm 13:6, he hath dealt bountifully with me.
Hebrew gamul (H1580) — a weaned child; Psalm 131:2, Isaiah 11:8, 28:9.
Hebrew shalav (H7961) — quiet, at ease; the settled state the psalm describes.
usage: “My soul is even as a weaned child” — present for the Person, not the provision.
“Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned” — a milestone worth celebrating.
“Them that are weaned from the milk” — who can receive the harder teaching.

pos: n. pl. (injuries to the flesh; rendering Hebrew chabburah, Greek trauma)
etymology: Old English wund. Scripture's wounds are inflicted by enemies, by friends, and — decisively — by the Servant's bearing of ours.
biblical_def: Wounds are injuries. Isaiah's Servant carries the definitive ones: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities… and with his stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5). Proverbs distinguishes their sources: “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (Pro 27:6). The Samaritan binds up a stranger's wounds, pouring in oil and wine (Luk 10:34), and Zechariah's Messiah is asked about “these wounds in thine hands” (Zec 13:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wound as a breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark and wood of a tree, or of the substance of other bodies, caused by violence.
webster_full: WOUND, n. A breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or of the bark and wood of a tree, or of the substance of other bodies, caused by violence or external force.
2. Injury; hurt; as a wound given to credit or reputation.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
Zec 13:6
And one shall say unto him, What are these wounds in thine hands? Then he shall answer, Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic culture treats all wounding as harm, which makes the faithful wounds of a friend indistinguishable from abuse — and leaves flattery unopposed.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 27:6 sets up a comparison most people get backwards: faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful. The friend inflicts pain and is trustworthy; the enemy gives affection and is lying. That single verse dismantles the assumption that the person who makes us feel worst has treated us worst. It also sets a test for the wounder: a faithful wound is aimed at healing and is delivered by someone who stays.

Isaiah 53:5 places the ultimate wounding beyond every human category. He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. The prepositions carry the doctrine — for our transgressions, not for His own; and the healing runs to us from injuries He absorbed. There is no other wound in Scripture that heals the person who did not receive it.
roots_summary: Hebrew chabburah (H2250), a stripe or bruise; chalal (H2490), to pierce or wound; Greek trauma (G5134), a wound.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to pierce, wound; Isaiah 53:5, he was wounded for our transgressions.
Hebrew chabburah (H2250) — stripe, bruise; Isaiah 53:5, with his stripes we are healed.
Greek trauma (G5134) — wound; Luke 10:34, bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine.
usage: “He was wounded for our transgressions” — injuries that heal another.
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” — the one who hurts may be the one who loves.
“Bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine” — the Samaritan's own supplies.

pos: v., n. (to crush; rendering Hebrew shuph and daka)
etymology: From Old French bruisier, to break. A bruise is damage under an unbroken surface — injury that does not show as a wound.
biblical_def: To bruise is to crush. The first gospel promise is stated in bruises: “it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” (Gen 3:15). Isaiah applies the verb to the Servant and to God's own purpose: “it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief” (Isa 53:10). And the promise of the Messiah's gentleness uses it too: “a bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench” (Isa 42:3), quoted of Christ in Matthew 12:20.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bruise as to crush by beating or pounding with an instrument not edged or pointed; and as a noun, a contusion.
webster_full: BRUISE, v.t. To crush by beating or pounding with an instrument not edged or pointed.
2. To crush by pressure.
BRUISE, n. A contusion; a hurt upon the flesh of animals, upon plants or other bodies, with a blunt or heavy instrument.
scriptures: Gen 3:15
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.

Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand.
Isa 42:3
A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth.
A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory.
corruption_summary: Christ's gentleness toward the bruised is preached without the cost that made it possible — He does not break the bruised reed because He was Himself bruised in their place.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3:15 uses one verb for two very different injuries, and the difference is anatomical. The serpent's head is bruised — a mortal blow; the seed's heel is bruised — a real wound, painful and costly, but not fatal. The first promise of the gospel therefore contains both the crucifixion and the resurrection in a single sentence, and it is spoken as a curse on the serpent rather than as comfort to the man and woman standing there.

Isaiah 42:3 and 53:10 belong together, and reading them apart weakens both. It pleased the LORD to bruise him — and a bruised reed shall he not break. The One who will not snap a damaged reed or pinch out a smoking wick is the same One whom it pleased the Father to crush. His tenderness toward the barely-alive is not temperament; it is purchased, and it is exercised by someone who knows the weight of the blow from the receiving end.
roots_summary: Hebrew shuph (H7779), to bruise or crush, in Genesis 3:15; daka (H1792), to crush, of the Servant in Isaiah 53:5,10; ratsats (H7533), to break in pieces.
roots_lines: Hebrew shuph (H7779) — to bruise, crush; Genesis 3:15, twice in one verse.
Hebrew daka (H1792) — to crush; Isaiah 53:5 and 53:10, it pleased the LORD to bruise him.
Hebrew ratsats (H7533) — to break, bruise; Isaiah 42:3, a bruised reed shall he not break.
usage: “It shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” — two injuries, one verb.
“It pleased the LORD to bruise him” — the Father's purpose in the crushing.
“A bruised reed shall he not break” — gentleness that cost Him everything.

pos: adj. (timid, losing courage; rendering Hebrew rak lebab, tender of heart)
etymology: Faint with heart — the translators' compound for a Hebrew idiom meaning soft-hearted in the sense of losing nerve.
biblical_def: Fainthearted means losing courage. The law makes remarkable provision for it: before a battle the officers proclaim, “What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart” (Deu 20:8). Isaiah tells Ahaz, “Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted” (Isa 7:4). Paul's word to the church is not dismissal but care: “comfort the feebleminded” (1Th 5:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fainthearted as cowardly, timorous, dejected, easily depressed or giving way to fear.
webster_full: FAINTHEARTED, a. Cowardly; timorous; dejected; easily depressed, or yielding to fear.
FAINTHEARTEDNESS, n. Cowardice; timorousness; want of courage.
scriptures: Deu 20:8

And the officers shall speak further unto the people, and they shall say, What man is there that is fearful and fainthearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart.
Isa 7:4
And say unto him, Take heed, and be quiet; fear not, neither be fainthearted for the two tails of these smoking firebrands, for the fierce anger of Rezin with Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.

And lest your heart faint, and ye fear for the rumour that shall be heard in the land; a rumour shall both come one year, and after that in another year shall come a rumour, and violence in the land, ruler against ruler.
corruption_summary: Fear is shamed rather than pastored, when the law itself made honourable provision for the fainthearted — and did so to protect the army, not to humiliate the man.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 20:8 is one of the most humane provisions in the law, and its reasoning is military rather than sentimental: let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart. Fear is treated as contagious, so the fearful man is sent home before the battle rather than exposed during it. He loses no standing; he is simply released. Any church culture that shames the frightened into staying in a fight they cannot sustain has ignored both halves of this — the mercy to the man and the protection of the ranks.

1 Thessalonians 5:14 shows the same discrimination in the New Testament: warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak. The fainthearted receive comfort, not warning. Getting this pairing right is most of pastoral wisdom, and getting it wrong — warning the fragile and comforting the rebellious — does damage that takes years to undo.
roots_summary: Hebrew rak lebab (H7390/H3824), tender or soft of heart — a battlefield idiom for lost nerve; Greek oligopsuchos (G3642), small-souled, in 1 Thessalonians 5:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; Deuteronomy 20:8, fearful and fainthearted.
Hebrew ragaz / rakak (H7401) — to be soft, faint; Isaiah 7:4, neither be fainthearted.
Greek oligopsuchos (G3642) — feebleminded, fainthearted; only 1 Thessalonians 5:14.
usage: “Let him go and return unto his house” — honourable release before the battle.
“Lest his brethren's heart faint as well” — fear is treated as contagious.
“Comfort the feebleminded” — the fainthearted get comfort, not warning.

etymology: Bare with foot. In the ancient world going unshod publicly signalled either mourning, captivity, or the presence of holiness.
biblical_def: Barefoot means unshod, and Scripture uses it for grief and for prophecy. David flees Absalom weeping, with his head covered, and “he went barefoot” (2Sa 15:30). Isaiah is commanded to walk “naked and barefoot three years for a sign” against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isa 20:2–3). At the bush Moses is told, “put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground” (Exo 3:5), and Joshua receives the same order before Jericho (Jos 5:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines barefoot as with the feet bare; without shoes or stockings.
webster_full: BAREFOOT, a. With the feet bare; without shoes or stockings.
BAREFOOT, adv. With the feet bare.
scriptures: And David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up. and
Isa 20:2
At the same time spake the LORD by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot.
Exo 3:5
And he said, Draw not nigh hither: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground.
Jos 5:15
And the captain of the LORD'S host said unto Joshua, Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy. And Joshua did so.
corruption_summary: Reverence has been redefined as a private inward attitude, where Scripture keeps assigning it a posture — and the first instruction at the burning bush concerned footwear.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 3:5 is worth noticing for what God does not say first. Before the name I AM, before the commission, before the promise of deliverance, comes an instruction about shoes: put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground. The ground was ordinary desert until God was in it. Holiness is not a property of the location but of the Presence, and the response required is bodily before it is theological.

David's barefoot ascent of Olivet is the other use. He went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up. A king walking unshod out of his own capital is enacted grief, public and undisguised — and centuries later Another would weep over the same city from the same hill.
roots_summary: Hebrew yacheph (H3182), barefoot; the removal of shoes also figures in the kinsman-redeemer transaction of Ruth 4:7.
roots_lines: Hebrew yacheph (H3182) — barefoot; 2 Samuel 15:30, Isaiah 20:2-4, Jeremiah 2:25.
Hebrew naal (H5275) — sandal, shoe; Exodus 3:5, Joshua 5:15, Ruth 4:7.
Hebrew shal (H7573) — to draw off; the verb of loosing the shoe at the bush.
usage: “Put off thy shoes from off thy feet” — the first instruction at the bush.
“He went barefoot” — a king's enacted grief on Olivet.
“Naked and barefoot three years for a sign” — Isaiah's costly obedience.

etymology: Old English swat. Sweat enters Scripture as part of the curse and reappears, decisively, in a garden at night.
biblical_def: Sweat is perspiration, and it is named in the sentence on Adam: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground” (Gen 3:19). Ezekiel's priests are to wear linen and “shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat” in the inner court (Eze 44:18). And Luke, a physician, records the Second Adam in Gethsemane: “being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luk 22:44).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sweat as the fluid or sensible moisture which is excreted from the skin of an animal; perspiration; and labor, toil, drudgery.
webster_full: SWEAT, n. The fluid or sensible moisture which is excreted from the skin of an animal; the fluid secreted by the perspiratory glands.
2. Labor; toil; drudgery.
3. Moisture issuing from any substance.
scriptures: Gen 3:19
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
They shall have linen bonnets upon their heads, and shall have linen breeches upon their loins; they shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat.
Gen 3:17

And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;
corruption_summary: Work is treated as either self-actualization or pure punishment, when Genesis places the sweat inside a curse on the ground rather than on labour itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The sentence in Genesis 3 is careful about its target: cursed is the ground for thy sake. Adam had been given work before the fall — to dress the garden and to keep it — so labour is not the curse; resistance is. Thorns and thistles, sweat, and futility enter a vocation that was already good. That distinction rescues work from being merely a penalty and keeps it from being idolized as the meaning of life.

Luke 22:44 places the Second Adam in a garden, sweating, and reverses the direction. Where the first Adam sweated because he had eaten what was forbidden, Christ sweats in agony before drinking a cup He did not deserve. Luke's clinical detail — as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground — puts the sweat back into the same soil that was cursed, which is where the curse began and where its remedy was purchased.
roots_summary: Hebrew zeah (H2188), sweat, in Genesis 3:19; yeza (H3154), that which causes sweat, in Ezekiel 44:18; Greek hidros (G2402) in Luke 22:44.
roots_lines: Hebrew zeah (H2188) — sweat; only Genesis 3:19, in the sweat of thy face.
Hebrew yeza (H3154) — sweat; only Ezekiel 44:18, of the priests' linen garments.
Greek hidros (G2402) — sweat; only Luke 22:44, his sweat was as it were great drops of blood.
usage: “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” — the ground cursed, not the work.
“His sweat was as it were great drops of blood” — the Second Adam in a garden.
“Shall not gird themselves with any thing that causeth sweat” — no strain in the inner court.
